chunks: "A charge pump moves charge with switches and capacitors to make a voltage that's a multiple of the input, with no inductor. Take a doubler.
In phase one, two switches connect the flying capacitor across the input, so it charges up to V in .
In phase two, the switches re-wire it so its bottom plate goes to V in and its top plate goes to the output.
Now the capacitor is stacked on top of the input source, so the output node sits at V in plus V in equals 2 volts in and the capacitor delivers its charge to the output capacitor and the load.
Then it flips back and recharges. The output capacitor holds the output steady between pulses. The thing to remember is that it isn't free energy.
Each cycle the flying capacitor takes a packet of charge from the input in phase one and again in phase two, so the input current is about twice the output current.
And the output isn't stiff: the more current you draw, the more the flying capacitor droops and the switch resistance drops voltage, so the output looks like 2 volts in minus I outR out .
That's why charge pumps suit low currents, tens to a few hundred milliamps."
